common_name: Dixie Crimson Clover (Earliest-Maturing Reseeding Southern Cover Crop Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in early fall; Dixie is the earliest-maturing of the classic reseeding crimson clovers, flowering and setting hard seed ahead of Auburn and Talladega.

directions: Dixie was released by the Georgia Experiment Station at Griffin and was one of the first crimson clovers bred for hard-seededness, a trait that lets a stand reseed itself year after year without annual replanting. It is the earliest-maturing of the reseeding crimson clovers, flowering and setting seed before Auburn, Chief, Kentucky Pride, and Talladega, which makes it well suited to rotations needing an early spring window for the next crop. Broadcast or drill seed onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in early fall so plants build a strong root system before winter, then either terminate at early bloom for maximum nitrogen release and biomass, or allow a portion of the stand to mature and shatter seed to sustain a self-reseeding planting in subsequent years. As with other crimson clovers it is a strong nitrogen-fixing legume and an excellent early-season pollinator resource.

common_name: Spooner Cereal Rye (University-Trialed Northern Cover Crop Rye)

planting.note: Sow in fall before or shortly after the first frost; Spooner is a cereal rye cultivar regularly included in northern cover crop variety trials for its stand establishment and winter survival.

directions: Spooner is a cereal rye cultivar evaluated alongside standards like Aroostook and Wheeler in University of Vermont Extension winter rye variety trials and other regional cover crop rye comparisons. Drill or broadcast into a prepared or lightly tilled fall seedbed; like other cereal ryes it establishes a dense, fibrous root system that scavenges residual nitrogen, suppresses weeds through winter, and produces a flush of biomass in spring. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or tilling at or before anthesis ahead of the following cash crop, since mature stands can be difficult to kill and may volunteer if allowed to set seed.

common_name: ND Dylan Winter Rye (NDSU-Bred High-Yield Cover Crop and Grain Rye)

planting.note: Sow in fall; ND Dylan was released by North Dakota State University and selected for very good winter hardiness and standability under Northern Plains conditions.

directions: ND Dylan is a tall, strong-strawed winter rye released by North Dakota State University and protected under Plant Variety Protection, sold only as certified seed. It combines high yield potential with very good early-season vigor and winter hardiness, making it suited to grain, forage, or cover crop use across the Northern Plains. NDSU research has used ND Dylan as a fall-seeded cover crop ahead of pinto bean production to reduce soil erosion and suppress weeds. Drill into a firm fall seedbed; terminate by mowing, rolling, or herbicide at or before heading if grown strictly as a cover crop, or allow it to mature for grain harvest in a dual-purpose system.

common_name: Musketeer Cereal Rye (Canadian-Bred Cover Crop and Grain Rye)

planting.note: Sow in fall; Musketeer is a Canadian-bred cereal rye variety included in regional Northeast cover crop rye trials.

directions: Musketeer is a cereal rye variety bred in Canada and evaluated in University of Vermont Extension Northwest Crops and Soils Program winter rye variety trials for yield and forage quality alongside cultivars like Aroostook and Wheeler. Drill or broadcast seed into a firm fall seedbed; it establishes quickly, provides strong ground cover and weed suppression through winter, and regrows vigorously in spring for either grazing, silage, or termination as a green manure ahead of a following crop. Terminate before heading to keep residue easy to manage and to avoid volunteer rye in the next planting.
sources: University of Vermont Extension Northwest Crops and Soils Program

common_name: Surpass BMR Sorghum-Sudangrass (High-Leaf Brown Midrib Forage and Cover Crop Hybrid)
scientific_name: Sorghum bicolor x Sorghum bicolor var. sudanense 'Surpass'

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past 65F and frost danger has passed; Surpass is a BMR6 (brown midrib) sorghum-sudangrass hybrid bred for a high leaf-to-stem ratio and easy dry-down.

directions: Surpass is a BMR6 (brown midrib) sorghum-sudangrass hybrid noted for a higher leaf-to-stem ratio and lower lignin content than standard BMR hybrid sorghums, giving it strong nonsenescent green-leaf retention and forage quality comparable to alfalfa through the season. Broadcast or drill seed into warm summer soil once soil temperatures are reliably above 65F, then mow at roughly knee height before seed heads emerge to keep growth leafy and stimulate dense regrowth for hay, baleage, silage, greenchop, or grazing. As a summer cover crop it produces heavy biomass quickly, suppresses warm-season weeds, and can be winterkilled or mowed and incorporated ahead of a fall planting.

common_name: FSG 208 BMR Sorghum-Sudangrass (Allied Seed Brown Midrib Forage and Cover Crop Hybrid)
scientific_name: Sorghum bicolor x Sorghum bicolor var. sudanense 'FSG 208'

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep between mid-spring and midsummer once soil has warmed; FSG 208 is an Allied Seed BMR sorghum-sudangrass hybrid selected for vigor and drought tolerance.

directions: FSG 208 is a brown midrib (BMR) hybrid sorghum-sudangrass bred by Allied Seed with excellent early vigor, drought tolerance, and strong regrowth potential for silage, hay, or grazing, along with high palatability and digestibility even when harvest is delayed past the optimum cutting stage. Plant about 1 inch deep between mid-spring and midsummer once soil has warmed; avoid soils with a high pH, where chlorosis can become a problem. As a summer cover crop it produces rapid, dense biomass that suppresses weeds and can be mowed for forage through the season before being winterkilled or incorporated ahead of a fall planting.

common_name: CCS-779 Tillage Radish (Original PVP-Protected Groff/Weil Daikon Cover Crop Radish)

planting.note: Sow 6-10 weeks before first frost; CCS-779 is the original plant-variety-protected daikon radish behind the Tillage Radish brand, developed by Ray Weil (University of Maryland) and no-till farmer Steve Groff.

directions: CCS-779 is the original daikon-type forage radish selection marketed as Tillage Radish, developed by University of Maryland soil scientist Ray Weil in collaboration with Pennsylvania no-till farmer Steve Groff and granted U.S. Plant Variety Protection. Broadcast seed about half an inch deep in late summer to early fall so plants form a large, deep taproot before winter; the root scavenges and holds nitrogen that would otherwise leach away, breaks up compacted soil layers, and improves water infiltration for the following crop. In climates cold enough for a hard freeze the roots winterkill and decompose in place, leaving open channels and releasing captured nutrients without any spring tillage or herbicide termination needed; in milder zones, mow before flowering to prevent volunteer seed set.

common_name: Maxum Field Pea (Rank-Growing Spring and Fall Cover Crop Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in late summer for a short-term fall cover; Maxum is a tall, rank-growing field pea bred for biomass rather than seed harvest, similar in use to 4010 field pea.

directions: Maxum is a tall, vigorous field pea marketed for short-term spring or fall green manure use, either alone or in mixes with oats, vetch, winter rye, or ryegrass. Sow in cool, moist soil; plants reach 2 to 3 feet and can be turned under 20-30 days after bloom for maximum nitrogen release, or harvested earlier as a quick-growing weed-suppressing cover. Like other forage-type field peas it has a shallow root system and limited drought tolerance, and it is not reliably winter-hardy in cold climates, so it is best used as a short-window spring or late-summer cover rather than an overwintering crop. As a legume it fixes nitrogen for the following cash crop and its young tendrils are also edible.

common_name: Vinter Hairy Vetch (Minnesota-Bred Extra-Winter-Hardy Cover Crop Vetch)

planting.note: Direct sow in mid to late summer in the Upper Midwest, ideally with a companion crop like rye or oats; Vinter was bred at the University of Minnesota specifically for superior winter survival in severe northern winters.

directions: Vinter was developed at the University of Minnesota from the most winter-hardy local hairy vetch ecotypes identified across multiple Minnesota winters, with seed from surviving plants composited and recurrently selected for vigor and fall/spring ground coverage. It is intended as a replacement for widely sold variety-not-stated hairy vetch seed in regions with severe winters, offering meaningfully better winter survival and heavier spring biomass. Broadcast or drill seed into a firm fall seedbed, inoculating with the appropriate rhizobium, and seed alongside a companion grain such as rye or oats to improve winter survival. Terminate at early bloom by mowing, rolling, or tilling before planting the following cash crop.
